title: Ingrid examines a prion sample
topic: A laboratory team investigates a prion sample: Ingrid receives a tissue sample with misfolded prions, the microscope shows fibrils that form a plaque, a chaperone protein dissolves an aggregate, a colleague disagrees with the result, and a second test confirms the prion
tail_E: Ingrid writes in her notes that the sheep suffered from a fatal prion
target_note: 'disease' is the natural completion of 'the sheep suffered from a fatal prion' after ten units about misfolded prions, fibrils and a plaque in sheep tissue: 'prion disease' is the standard collocation of the domain, and the tail fixes the slot after 'a fatal prion' to a noun. The word occurs nowhere in the units or the tail (no 'disease', 'diseases', 'diseased'), and neither does a German equivalent (Krankheit / Erkrankung / Leiden); 'illness' and 'infection' are also absent, so the competing continuations are not primed either. ' disease' is a single Pythia token (id 2728); Pythia-160m ranks it first after the all-English context (p ~ 0.45, next candidates 'infection' ~ 0.16 and 'illness' ~ 0.06)
author: LS-NEQ stimulus authoring (F19A, prion sample in the laboratory, Ingrid)
notes: Formulation A, domain protein_misfolding (DESIGN.md §4.8: misfolded proteins are the proposed counter-pole to the culture/politics families F13-F16, from the PubMed side of the Pile; whether misfolding really is the hardest subdomain is measured there, not assumed here). Ten meaning units: Ingrid receives a tissue sample / the sample contains misfolded prions from a sheep / she puts it under the microscope / the microscope shows fibrils / the fibrils form a plaque between the cells / Ingrid mixes in a chaperone protein / the chaperone dissolves an aggregate / a colleague disagrees at the meeting / Ingrid repeats the test / the second test confirms the prion. Domain vocabulary in both languages: prion/Prion(en), misfolded/fehlgefaltet, fibril/Fibrille, plaque/Plaque, chaperone protein/Chaperonprotein, aggregate/Aggregat. The German compound is written closed ('Chaperonprotein', not 'Chaperon-Protein') because lsne.lang_id groups tokens into words at a hyphen, so the second element 'Protein' would be read on its own as the English lexicon word and would break the language-ID switch count. Subjects alternate between the protagonist (Ingrid), a colleague, and objects of the experiment (the sample, the microscope, the fibrils, the chaperone, the second test), singular and plural, so C3 switches cross real subject-verb agreement. No separable German verbs ('hinzugeben', 'auflösen', 'nachweisen' avoided: 'mischt ... in', 'löst', 'bestätigt'; 'widerspricht' and 'wiederholt' are inseparable). Present tense, positive polarity throughout; unit 9 reads naturally in German, units 1 and 10 in English, unit 10 is the closing sentence. 'Ingrid' is the only proper name and is not in the lexicon's name list (data/lexicon/function_words.json, key 'N'); it is cue-less and capitalised, so lsne.lang_id labels it 'N' (excluded from the accuracy counts) rather than 'E' or 'D' - no lexicon edit was needed, and the language-ID tests pass unchanged.
